title: Resilience: timeouts, retries, circuit breaker, bulkhead, load shedding, backpressure
scopeHtml: Scope: Timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breaker, bulkhead, load shedding, backpressure, fallbacks, combining patterns.

notes.title: Why resilience patterns exist
notes.html:
In a system of many services, something is always failing; resilience is making sure one slow or broken piece does not take everything down.

The key danger is the cascading failure: Service B becomes slow, so A's threads pile up waiting for B, A runs out of threads and becomes slow, so C (which calls A) piles up, and the whole fleet dies though only B was sick. Slowness is worse than a clean failure, because it holds resources.

Availability math. If a request calls 5 services in series each at 99.9%, the result is 0.999^5 = 99.5%, i.e. about 3.6 hours of downtime per month instead of 43 minutes. Resilience patterns keep a degraded dependency from dragging the whole request down.

Toolbox covered here, roughly in order of use:

  1. Timeouts (never wait forever).
  2. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter.
  3. Circuit breakers (stop calling a failing dependency).
  4. Bulkheads (isolate resources per dependency).
  5. Load shedding and rate limiting (refuse excess work early).
  6. Backpressure (tell producers to slow down).
  7. Fallbacks and graceful degradation.

Industry examples. Netflix's Hystrix (now in maintenance; Resilience4j is the common JVM successor), Amazon's Builders' Library articles on timeouts, retries and backoff, and shedding load; Envoy and Istio provide most of these at the proxy layer.

Everyday analogy. House fuse boxes: a faulty kettle trips its own circuit rather than burning the whole building.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding retries first; without timeouts and limits they make outages worse.
  • Describing patterns in isolation instead of how they combine.

notes.title: Timeouts
notes.html:
A timeout is the maximum time you will wait for a response. Without one, a hung dependency can hold your thread forever.

Types: connect timeout (small, e.g. 100 to 500 ms in a datacenter), read/response timeout (based on the dependency's p99 or p99.9), and an overall deadline for the whole user request.

How to choose: set the timeout just above the dependency's observed p99.9 latency, e.g. p99 = 120 ms, p99.9 = 300 ms, timeout = 400 to 500 ms. Too tight causes false failures; too loose lets resources be held.

Deadline propagation. If the user request has a 2 s budget and the first hop used 1.2 s, the next hop should get only 800 ms remaining, not a fresh 2 s. gRPC does this natively (deadlines); with HTTP pass a header or context. This avoids work whose answer nobody is waiting for.

// OkHttp: connect, read and an overall call timeout
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .readTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .callTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)   // whole call incl. retries by interceptors
    .build()
# Envoy route timeout (illustrative)
route:
  timeout: 2s
  retry_policy: { retry_on: "5xx,reset", num_retries: 1, per_try_timeout: 0.8s }

Worked example. Thread pool of 200, calls at 500 req/s with a healthy 40 ms latency need 500 x 0.04 = 20 busy threads (Little's law: L = lambda x W). If the dependency hangs with no timeout, in 0.4 s all 200 threads are stuck. With a 500 ms timeout the pool still saturates under a hard hang: 500 req/s x 0.5 s = 250 threads wanted. This is why timeouts need breakers and bulkheads too.

Industry examples. Amazon recommends setting timeouts from the downstream p99.9 and tracking time-outs as a metric; JDBC drivers, HTTP clients and Kafka clients all have defaults that are often infinite or very large (for example some HTTP clients default to no read timeout), so always set them explicitly.

Decision gravity. Timeouts are cheap and reversible; getting them wrong silently is the risk. Review them whenever dependency latency changes.

Everyday analogy. Hanging up if nobody answers after 10 rings, instead of holding the phone all day.

Common interview traps.

  • Using the default (infinite) timeout.
  • Timeouts that are longer than the caller's own timeout, so work continues after the caller gave up.
  • Retrying non-idempotent writes after a timeout (the first attempt may have succeeded).

notes.title: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter
notes.html:
A retry repeats a failed call because many failures are transient. Done naively it multiplies load on a struggling dependency and can cause a retry storm.

Rules:

  1. Retry only transient errors (timeouts, 503, connection reset), not 4xx client errors.
  2. Retry only idempotent operations, or use an idempotency key (Stripe's Idempotency-Key).
  3. Use exponential backoff: delay = base x 2^attempt (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms...), capped (e.g. 10 s).
  4. Add jitter: randomise the delay so clients do not retry in sync. "Full jitter": sleep = random(0, min(cap, base x 2^attempt)).
  5. Limit attempts (2 or 3 total) and use a retry budget (retries <= 10% of normal request volume).
  6. Retry at ONE layer, not at every layer.
import random, time

def call_with_retry(fn, attempts=3, base=0.1, cap=5.0):
    for n in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except TransientError:
            if n == attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** n)))  # full jitter

Retry amplification. If 3 layers each retry 3 times, one user request becomes up to 27 calls to the bottom service during an outage, exactly when it can least cope. A 1,000 req/s service in trouble sees 3,000 to 27,000 req/s.

Worked example. 10,000 clients get a failure at t=0. Without jitter and a 1 s backoff, all 10,000 retry at t=1 s (a spike). With full jitter over 0 to 1 s, about 10 per ms, a smooth ramp the service can absorb.

Industry examples. AWS SDKs use exponential backoff with jitter by default (the AWS Architecture Blog post "Exponential Backoff and Jitter" compared the strategies); gRPC has retry policies with throttling; Google's SRE book describes retry budgets; Stripe and Square rely on idempotency keys for safe retries.

Decision gravity. A retry policy is reversible config, but unbounded retries during an outage can turn a partial failure into a total one; put the budget in the shared client library.

Everyday analogy. Redialing a busy number: if everyone calls back at exactly the same second, the line stays busy; waiting a random while helps.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying without jitter.
  • Retrying at every layer.
  • Retrying POST payment calls without idempotency keys, causing double charges.
  • Retrying on 4xx or on non-transient errors.

notes.title: Circuit breaker
notes.html:
A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing, so callers fail fast and the dependency gets time to recover.

Three states:

  • Closed: requests flow; failures are counted.
  • Open: requests are rejected immediately (or served from fallback) for a cool-down period (e.g. 30 s).
  • Half-open: after the cool-down, allow a few trial requests; if they succeed, close; if not, open again.

Trip rule examples: failure rate above 50% over the last 20 calls (sliding window) with at least 10 calls, or slow-call rate above 80% for calls over 1 s.

# Resilience4j-style configuration (Spring Boot)
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.payments:
  slidingWindowType: COUNT_BASED
  slidingWindowSize: 20
  minimumNumberOfCalls: 10
  failureRateThreshold: 50
  slowCallDurationThreshold: 1s
  slowCallRateThreshold: 80
  waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
  permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 3

Worked example. Recommendation service goes down. Without a breaker each page load waits 2 s for a timeout then shows nothing: p99 = 2 s, threads pinned. With a breaker open, calls fail in under 1 ms and the page shows a cached "popular items" list. Latency recovers instantly and the recommender faces zero load while it restarts.

Where to put it. In the client library or the service mesh sidecar (Envoy's outlier detection ejects bad hosts; connection-pool circuit breakers limit pending requests). Use one breaker per dependency (or per endpoint), not one global.

Industry examples. Netflix Hystrix popularised it; Resilience4j on JVM; Polly on .NET; Istio/Envoy outlier detection; Android apps use breaker-like logic to stop hitting a failing API and show cached content.

Decision gravity. Easy to add, reversible; the risk is wrong thresholds (flapping or never tripping). Combine with a meaningful fallback, otherwise "fail fast" still fails.

Everyday analogy. The household fuse: after a surge it cuts the circuit, and you test it carefully before turning everything on again.

Common interview traps.

  • A breaker with no fallback and no metrics on state changes.
  • A global breaker shared by unrelated endpoints.
  • Setting the cool-down so short that it hammers the recovering service.

notes.title: Bulkheads
notes.html:
A bulkhead isolates resources into separate compartments so a failure in one cannot sink the rest. Named after ship hull compartments.

Forms:

  • Thread pool / semaphore per dependency: the payments client gets 20 threads, the recommendations client 10. If recommendations hangs, at most 10 threads are lost.
  • Connection pool per dependency or per tenant.
  • Separate processes or deployments: run admin or batch traffic on separate instances from user traffic.
  • Per-tenant or per-shard isolation (cell-based architecture): noisy tenant A cannot starve tenant B.
  • Separate queues for priorities (critical vs bulk emails).
// Resilience4j semaphore bulkhead: max 10 concurrent calls, wait up to 50 ms
BulkheadConfig cfg = BulkheadConfig.custom()
    .maxConcurrentCalls(10)
    .maxWaitDuration(Duration.ofMillis(50))
    .build();
Bulkhead recsBulkhead = Bulkhead.of("recs", cfg);

Worked example. Shared pool of 200 threads and recs hangs: all 200 get stuck within seconds, checkout fails too. With bulkheads, recs maxes out at 10 threads; checkout still has 100+ threads and keeps working; recommendations show a fallback.

Industry examples. AWS cell-based architecture (a cell is a self-contained shard of the stack; failures stay within a cell, e.g. Route 53 and many internal services use cells); Slack and DoorDash discuss cell architectures; Kubernetes resource limits and namespaces provide process-level isolation; Android uses separate executors/dispatchers for IO, DB and network so one cannot block the others.

Decision gravity. More isolation means worse average utilisation (idle reserved capacity) but a lower worst case. Cell-based architecture is a one-way door at the infrastructure level (it reshapes routing and data layout).

Everyday analogy. A ship's watertight compartments: one flooded section does not sink the vessel.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing pools by guess; size them from Little's law (concurrency = rate x latency) plus headroom.
  • Forgetting that a shared database connection pool is also a shared fate.

notes.title: Load shedding and rate limiting
notes.html:
Load shedding means deliberately rejecting some requests when the system is overloaded, so that the rest are still served quickly. Without it, every request gets slow (latency explodes) and then nobody gets a useful answer.

Why it is needed: past about 100% utilisation queues grow without bound; waiting time rises sharply as utilisation approaches 1 (queueing theory, roughly 1/(1-rho)). Users also retry, adding load.

Techniques:

  • Reject early (at the edge or the start of the handler) with HTTP 503 / 429 and Retry-After, cheaper than doing half the work.
  • Rate limiting: token bucket per client/API key (e.g. 100 req/s, burst 200).
  • Concurrency limits: adaptive (Netflix's concurrency-limits uses TCP-Vegas/AIMD-like algorithms to find the limit from latency).
  • Prioritised shedding: drop low-priority traffic first (analytics, prefetch, bulk), keep checkout and login. Google and Facebook tag requests by criticality.
  • Drop queued requests whose deadline has passed (the client already gave up: LIFO queue or CoDel-style drop).
  • Server-side queue time limit: reject if the request has waited longer than X ms.
# NGINX: limit each client IP to 10 req/s with a burst of 20, reject the rest quickly
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m rate=10r/s;
server {
  location /api/ {
    limit_req zone=perip burst=20 nodelay;
    limit_req_status 429;
  }
}

Worked example. Capacity 1,000 req/s; a spike brings 1,500 req/s. Without shedding, the 500 extra queue, latency climbs from 50 ms to many seconds, timeouts trigger retries, and goodput falls toward zero. With shedding, 1,000 req/s are served fast and 500 get a quick 503: roughly 67% success instead of near 0%.

Industry examples. Google SRE describes client-side adaptive throttling and criticality-based shedding; Amazon's Builders' Library "Using load shedding to avoid overload"; Stripe uses several rate limiter types (request rate, concurrent requests, fleet usage load shedder, worker utilisation shedder); Cloudflare and API gateways rate-limit by key.

Decision gravity. Shedding is a product decision (which users or features lose first); implementing it early is cheap, retrofitting priority classes across services is expensive.

Everyday analogy. A club bouncer who stops letting people in when it is full instead of letting everyone crush inside.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing "scale out" removes the need for shedding (autoscaling takes minutes).
  • Shedding after expensive work is already done.
  • No Retry-After / backoff signal to clients, so they retry immediately.

notes.title: Backpressure
notes.html:
Backpressure is a slow consumer telling a fast producer to slow down, so queues do not grow until memory runs out.

Without backpressure: a producer writes 10,000 msg/s into an in-memory queue while the consumer handles 2,000 msg/s; the queue grows by 8,000 msg/s and the process hits OOM or latency becomes minutes.

Mechanisms:

  • Bounded queues that block or reject when full (ArrayBlockingQueue, bounded channels).
  • Pull-based consumption: consumers pull what they can handle (Kafka consumers poll; SQS long polling).
  • Credit-based flow control: receiver grants credits (TCP window, HTTP/2 flow control, gRPC, RSocket, Reactive Streams request(n)).
  • Rate limiting or HTTP 429/503 to signal upstream.
  • Drop or sample when data is loss tolerant (metrics, telemetry).
// Kotlin Flow / channels: a bounded buffer suspends the producer instead of growing forever
val ch = Channel<Event>(capacity = 100)               // bounded
launch { for (e in source) ch.send(e) }               // send suspends when full
launch { for (e in ch) process(e) }                   // slow consumer paces the producer

Worked example. Kafka consumers lag: producer 50 MB/s, consumers 30 MB/s; the topic retains data on disk so lag grows 20 MB/s (72 GB/hour) but the system survives (disk is the buffer), and you add consumers or partitions. The in-memory version of the same mismatch would crash in seconds. Metric: consumer lag and age of oldest message.

Industry examples. TCP itself; Reactive Streams (RxJava, Reactor, Akka Streams) with request(n); Kotlin Flow and channels with buffer overflow strategies (SUSPEND, DROP_OLDEST); Kafka as a durable buffer; Android Flow.conflate() to drop intermediate UI states.

Decision gravity. Choose per stream: block (never lose, add latency), drop (lose data, keep latency), or buffer (hide the problem until memory is gone). Explicitly choose; defaults are often unbounded.

Everyday analogy. A factory conveyor belt where the packer presses a stop button when the boxes pile up, instead of the belt dumping boxes on the floor.

Common interview traps.

  • Unbounded queues anywhere (thread pool executor with unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue).
  • Confusing backpressure with load shedding: backpressure slows the sender; shedding drops work.
  • Autoscaling consumers without checking the downstream they write to.

notes.title: Fallbacks and graceful degradation
notes.html:
A fallback is the plan B when a dependency fails: serve something less perfect instead of an error.

Options, from best to worst:

  1. Cached/stale data (stale-while-revalidate): product page from cache when the catalog is slow.
  2. Default values: generic recommendations ("top 10") instead of personalised.
  3. Feature disable: hide the non-essential widget.
  4. Queue for later: accept the order and process asynchronously.
  5. Fail clearly with a friendly error and retry later.

Rules: fall back only to something safe; never "fail open" for security (do not skip auth if the auth service is down) unless explicitly accepted; test fallbacks regularly (chaos testing) because untested fallbacks are broken.

Worked example. Product page needs price, reviews and recommendations. Price (critical) failing = error; reviews failing = hide section; recs failing = show bestsellers. Availability of the page = availability of price alone (say 99.95%) instead of the product of three (about 99.85%).

Chaos engineering. Deliberately inject failures to verify the patterns work: Netflix Chaos Monkey (kills instances), Gremlin, AWS Fault Injection Service, Litmus for Kubernetes. Start in staging, then small production experiments with a stop button.

Industry examples. Netflix shows a generic row if personalisation fails; Amazon's homepage degrades components independently; mobile apps show cached feeds when offline.

Decision gravity. Deciding which features are critical versus optional is a product architecture decision, best done up front, and affects data and API design (separate endpoints let you fail independently).

Everyday analogy. When the elevator is broken, there are stairs: slower, but you still arrive.

Common interview traps.

  • Fallback that calls the same failing dependency again.
  • Never testing the fallback path.
  • Treating every dependency as critical.

notes.title: Putting it together
notes.html:
A robust call from service A to service B, outermost to innermost:

  1. Rate limit / admission control on A's own inbound traffic.
  2. Bulkhead around calls to B (limit concurrency).
  3. Circuit breaker around B (fail fast when B is sick).
  4. Retry (max 2 more attempts, backoff + jitter, idempotent only, budgeted).
  5. Timeout per attempt, within the overall deadline.
  6. Fallback if everything fails.

Order matters: a retry wraps the timeout; the breaker records the outcome of the retried call or each attempt (library dependent; confirm your library's decorator order).

Observability: emit metrics for breaker state, retries, timeouts, shed requests, bulkhead rejections and queue depth; alert on SLO burn, not on each pattern firing.

Worked incident (metastable failure). A short traffic spike caused timeouts, clients retried, the extra load kept the system overloaded even after the original spike ended: it stayed down until retries were blocked and load dropped. Fix: retry budgets, load shedding, and a manual "circuit" to stop traffic while caches warm up. Keywords: retry storm, metastable failure.

Industry examples. Envoy/Istio provides timeouts, retries, outlier detection, and circuit breaking in one place; Resilience4j decorators on JVM; Polly on .NET.

Decision gravity. Prefer shared libraries or a service mesh so every team gets the same defaults; per-team ad hoc settings drift and fail in different ways. Moving them into a mesh later is a medium-effort change.

Common interview traps.

  • Listing all patterns without ordering or limits.
  • Forgetting to test under overload (load tests with a failing dependency).
  • Setting retry count and timeouts independently, so total time exceeds the user's patience.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• One slow dependency causes cascading failure; slowness is worse than failure because it holds resources. Series availability multiplies down.
  • Timeouts everywhere, set from the downstream p99.9, with deadline propagation.
  • Retries: transient and idempotent only, exponential backoff with full jitter, small budget, at one layer. Beware retry amplification and retry storms.
  • Circuit breaker: closed, open, half-open; per dependency; pair with a fallback.
  • Bulkheads isolate pools per dependency or tenant; cell-based architecture is the extreme.
  • Load shedding rejects early to preserve goodput; prioritise criticality; use Retry-After.
  • Backpressure bounds queues and slows producers; never use unbounded queues.
  • Graceful degradation and chaos testing prove the plan B works.

questions.promptHtml: What is a cascading failure, and why is a slow dependency often worse than a dead one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who know "services fail" from those who know how failure spreads through resource exhaustion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A cascading failure is when one sick service makes its callers sick, which makes their callers sick. A dead dependency fails fast and frees the caller's thread. A slow one holds the thread, so callers run out of threads or connections, become slow themselves, and the whole chain collapses although only one service was unhealthy. Resilience patterns exist to cap how long and how much we wait.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client -> A (threads blocked) -> B (threads blocked) -> C slow

Little's law: busy threads = rate x latency. At 500 req/s and 40 ms you need 20 threads. If C slows to 2 s you need 1,000 threads; a pool of 200 is exhausted in under half a second, so A now fails everything, including requests that never touch C. Availability multiplies in series: 5 calls at 99.9% each give 0.999^5 = 99.5%, about 3.6 hours down per month instead of 43 minutes. Toolbox in order of use: timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding, backpressure, fallbacks.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding retries first; without timeouts and budgets they make outages worse.
  • Describing each pattern alone rather than how they combine.
  • Thinking "more instances" fixes it; the caller's pool exhaustion is per instance.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do timeouts alone not suffice? -> A hard hang still fills the pool within the timeout window (500 req/s x 0.5 s = 250 threads wanted); you also need breakers and bulkheads.
  2. How does a service mesh help? -> Envoy/Istio give timeouts, retries, outlier detection and connection-pool limits uniformly.
  3. What metric shows it starting? -> Rising thread pool active count, queue depth and in-flight requests before error rate moves.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use a circuit breaker". Senior: explains resource exhaustion with Little's law and layers several patterns with limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An outage of a minor recommendations service took down checkout because both shared one HTTP client pool.

questions.promptHtml: How do you choose a timeout for a downstream call, and what is deadline propagation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Default timeouts are often infinite; seniors set them from data and budget them across hops.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I set connect timeouts small (100 to 500 ms in a datacenter) and the read timeout just above the dependency's observed p99.9, for example p99.9 = 300 ms gives 400 to 500 ms. On top I keep one overall deadline for the user request and pass the remaining budget downstream, so the next hop gets 800 ms left, not a fresh 2 s. That stops work nobody is waiting for.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Too tight causes false failures; too loose holds resources. gRPC propagates deadlines natively; over HTTP pass a header or context.

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .readTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .callTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .build()
OkHttpClient client = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .readTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .callTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .build();
Client 2 s -> A (1.5 s left) -> B (0.8 s left) -> DB

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using library defaults (some have no read timeout).
  • A callee timeout longer than the caller's, so work continues after the caller left.
  • Retrying a non-idempotent write after a timeout; the first attempt may have succeeded.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why p99.9 and not average? -> Average hides the tail that causes thread build-up.
  2. What if p99.9 is 5 s? -> Question the dependency and design async or fallback; do not make everyone wait 5 s.
  3. How do timeouts interact with retries? -> Retries must fit inside the deadline: attempts x per-try timeout <= budget.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "set a timeout of 5 seconds". Senior: data-derived values, per-try vs overall, propagation, and alerting on timeout rate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A JDBC pool with an infinite socket timeout froze 200 threads on a half-open connection after a network blip.

questions.promptHtml: Explain exponential backoff with jitter and why retries can make an outage worse.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Retry storms are a top cause of prolonged outages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Retries help only for transient, idempotent failures. I use exponential backoff capped at some maximum, with full jitter (sleep random between 0 and the current backoff) so clients do not retry in sync, limit to 2 or 3 attempts, add a retry budget of about 10% of normal traffic, and retry at one layer only. Without these, three layers each retrying three times turn one request into 27 calls just when the dependency is weakest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
import random, time
def call_with_retry(fn, attempts=3, base=0.1, cap=5.0):
    for n in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except TransientError:
            if n == attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** n)))

Worked example: 10,000 clients fail at t=0. No jitter and 1 s backoff: all 10,000 retry at t=1 s. Full jitter over 0 to 1 s: about 10 per ms, a smooth ramp. Idempotency: use an Idempotency-Key for POSTs (the Stripe pattern) so a retry after a lost response does not double charge.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Retrying 4xx or non-transient errors.
  • Retrying at every layer (amplification).
  • Retrying payments without idempotency keys.
  • Unbounded attempts with no budget.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a retry budget? -> A cap such as retries <= 10% of requests, so retries cannot more than add 10% load.
  2. Why full jitter rather than equal jitter? -> Full jitter spreads best and was shown to reduce total contention in the AWS analysis.
  3. How do you retry safely behind a mesh and in the client? -> Pick one layer; disable the other.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "retry three times". Senior: classifies errors, adds jitter, budget, idempotency and single-layer ownership.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A brief DB failover became a 40-minute outage as 3 layers of retries kept the new primary saturated.

questions.promptHtml: How does a circuit breaker work, and what makes a good configuration?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates know the states but not thresholds, scoping, or the fallback requirement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It has three states. Closed: calls flow and failures are counted. Open: calls are rejected immediately for a cool-down such as 30 s. Half-open: a few trial calls are allowed; success closes it, failure re-opens it. I trip on failure rate (say over 50% across the last 20 calls with at least 10 calls) and on slow-call rate, one breaker per dependency, and I always pair it with a fallback and emit state-change metrics.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.payments:
  slidingWindowType: COUNT_BASED
  slidingWindowSize: 20
  minimumNumberOfCalls: 10
  failureRateThreshold: 50
  slowCallDurationThreshold: 1s
  slowCallRateThreshold: 80
  waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
  permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 3

Effect: recommendations go down; without a breaker each page waits 2 s then shows nothing; with a breaker open, calls fail in under 1 ms and a cached "popular items" list appears, and the dependency receives zero load while it restarts. Placement: client library or mesh sidecar (Envoy outlier detection ejects bad hosts).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No fallback and no metrics on state changes.
  • One global breaker for unrelated endpoints.
  • A cool-down so short it hammers a recovering service.
  • Counting 4xx client errors as failures.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Breaker vs retry? -> Retry handles transient blips; the breaker stops retrying when failure is persistent.
  2. Time-based vs count-based windows? -> Count-based is simple; time-based is better at variable traffic; low traffic needs a minimum-calls rule.
  3. What is flapping and how do you reduce it? -> Rapid open/close from noisy thresholds; use larger windows, longer open time and multiple half-open probes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists the states. Senior: scopes per dependency, tunes thresholds from traffic, ties to a fallback and monitors state changes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A global breaker shared by search and checkout opened on search errors and blocked purchases.

questions.contextHtml: A user service at normal 1,200 req/s depends on an inventory service. At 09:12 inventory briefly slows (a 40 s GC pause). Afterwards inventory CPU stays at 100% and its request rate reads 9,800 req/s for 25 minutes even though user-facing traffic is flat at 1,200 req/s. Config: the mobile app retries 3 times with no delay; the API gateway retries 2 times on 5xx; the user service HTTP client retries 3 times with a fixed 100 ms delay. Inventory p99 is 6 s, caller timeout is 2 s.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the numbers and how you recover and prevent.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Inventory is overloaded, scale it up." Does not notice the load is self-inflicted amplification.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where are retries configured (client, gateway, service, mesh)? Are the operations idempotent? Is inventory still slow from real load or from backlog? What are the timeouts per layer?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cut retries at the gateway and client via config; shed or rate-limit traffic to inventory; open the circuit manually; add temporary capacity only after load drops.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) multiplicative retries: up to 4 x 3 x 3 = 36 attempts per user action (the 8x observed is consistent with partial amplification); (b) no jitter synchronises retries into waves; (c) timeouts shorter than server latency (2 s vs 6 s p99) so callers abandon work that the server still does, wasting capacity; (d) a real traffic increase (ruled out: flat 1,200 req/s).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare gateway, service and inventory request counts per layer; trace sampling showing repeated spans; check Retry-After and attempt headers; inventory queue depth and abandoned request counts.
  5. Root cause: A metastable retry storm: the trigger (GC pause) ended, but retry load kept inventory above capacity, so latency stayed above timeouts, causing more retries.
  6. Fix: Short term: remove retries from two layers, keep one with jitter, cap at 2 attempts. Long term: retry budget (<= 10%), circuit breaker, server-side load shedding with 503 plus Retry-After, drop requests whose deadline has expired, align timeouts so the callee's limit is below the caller's.
  7. Prevention: Load test with an injected 30 s dependency stall; alert on request amplification ratio (downstream rps / upstream rps); a client library enforcing budgets.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "just scale inventory" (the retry load scales up with you). Removing retries from the mobile app lowers resilience to real network blips; keep one jittered retry there.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retries are in a mesh we do not own? -> Configure per-route retry policy and budget, or turn it off centrally.
  • How do you stop a storm already running? -> Reduce incoming load temporarily (shed 50%) until the queue drains, then ramp.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 4-second blip became a 25-minute outage; only blocking traffic at the gateway for 90 seconds broke the loop.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale it up.
  • Hire: finds amplification and fixes retry config.
  • Strong hire: names metastability, quantifies amplification, adds budgets, shedding and a repeatable fault-injection test.

questions.contextHtml: A checkout service uses one shared thread pool of 200 for three dependencies: payments (p99 120 ms, 300 req/s), recommendations (p99 800 ms, 600 req/s) and email (p99 300 ms, 100 req/s). Last Friday recommendations hung and checkout failed for 18 minutes. You are asked to split the pool. Leadership wants "the minimum extra capacity".
questions.promptHtml: Size the bulkheads with numbers, and describe the trade-off.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Give each a pool of 66." Guesses and ignores Little's law and criticality.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which dependency is critical? What is acceptable behaviour when recs is full (drop, fallback)? Are these averages or p99? Is calling email necessary in the request path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a timeout on recs (say 300 ms) and a breaker with a fallback right now; move email to a queue.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Concurrency need = rate x latency. Payments: 300 x 0.12 = 36 (use p99 for headroom and add 50%, so about 55). Recs: 600 x 0.8 = 480 threads at p99 (clearly more than the whole pool!); but with a 300 ms timeout and a bounded semaphore of 20 it caps at 20, the rest take fallback. Email: 100 x 0.3 = 30; moving it async removes it from the pool.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check actual in-flight distribution from metrics (not just p99); load-test with recs hung; review bulkhead rejection rates.
  5. Root cause: One shared pool meant the slowest, least important dependency consumed 100% of capacity.
  6. Fix: Payments 60 threads (protected), recs semaphore 20 with 50 ms max wait and a fallback, email via queue; total pool 120 is enough. Remaining capacity reserved.
BulkheadConfig cfg = BulkheadConfig.custom()
    .maxConcurrentCalls(20)
    .maxWaitDuration(Duration.ofMillis(50))
    .build();
Bulkhead recs = Bulkhead.of("recs", cfg);
val cfg = BulkheadConfig.custom()
    .maxConcurrentCalls(20)
    .maxWaitDuration(Duration.ofMillis(50))
    .build()
val recs = Bulkhead.of("recs", cfg)
  1. Prevention: Dashboards for bulkhead saturation and rejection; load tests with each dependency hung in turn; also bulkhead the DB connection pool.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Isolation lowers average utilisation (reserved idle capacity) in return for a better worst case. Not oversized pools "just in case".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Per-tenant isolation? -> Per-tenant pools or cells so one noisy tenant cannot starve others.
  • Semaphore or thread-pool bulkhead? -> Semaphore is cheap and keeps the caller thread; a thread pool adds isolation and its own timeout at a context-switch cost.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After bulkheads, a hung recs API cost 20 threads and a blank widget instead of a full outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: equal split.
  • Hire: sizes via Little's law and protects the critical path.
  • Strong hire: finds the numbers are inconsistent with the timeout, moves email async, and tests each failure mode.

questions.contextHtml: An API has capacity of 1,000 req/s (autoscaler needs about 4 minutes to add pods). A marketing push brings 1,500 req/s for 20 minutes. Metrics during the first 5 minutes: CPU 100%, queue wait 9 s, p50 latency 11 s, error rate 0.5% but the success rate by users is dropping because clients time out at 3 s and retry. Goodput (responses delivered within 3 s) is about 60 req/s. The team proposes "just raise the autoscaler max".
questions.promptHtml: What do you do now and how do you design for this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale out." The scaling takes 4 minutes and does nothing for the live queue.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which endpoints are essential (login, checkout) vs optional? Do clients honour Retry-After? Is there a gateway? Are requests idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reject excess at the edge: 503/429 with Retry-After once the queue wait passes a limit (for example 200 ms), prioritise checkout and drop analytics and prefetch; drop queued requests older than the client timeout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Queueing: with utilisation above 1 the queue grows without bound; waiting time rises sharply near 1/(1-rho). Requests that finish after the client gave up are wasted work, so goodput collapses (60 req/s) though CPU is 100%.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare server-side completion rate with client-observed success; look at queue wait and in-flight metrics; check for retries per user.
  5. Root cause: Accepting more work than capacity, with no admission control, so every request becomes slow and useless.
  6. Fix: Admission control with a queue-time limit, concurrency limit (adaptive limits as in Netflix's concurrency-limits), per-key rate limits (token bucket, for example 100 req/s with burst 200), criticality tiers, and cheap rejection before expensive work.
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=perip:10m rate=10r/s;
location /api/ {
  limit_req zone=perip burst=20 nodelay;
  limit_req_status 429;
}

With shedding the service serves 1,000 req/s quickly (about 67% of users succeed) instead of near zero. 7. Prevention: Load test at 150% capacity; pre-scale for scheduled campaigns; autoscale on queue depth or concurrency not just CPU. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Shedding is a product decision (who loses first). Do not rely on autoscaling alone; and do not shed after doing expensive work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Clients ignore Retry-After? -> Enforce at the gateway, add client SDK backoff, ban abusive keys.
  • Fairness across tenants? -> Per-tenant quotas so one tenant cannot consume the whole shed budget.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch at 1.5x capacity yielded a 3% success rate until a 30-line admission filter returned 503 in under 2 ms for the excess.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale out.
  • Hire: shedding with Retry-After and priorities.
  • Strong hire: explains goodput collapse, drops expired work and adds adaptive concurrency limits.

questions.contextHtml: An ingestion service reads events from an HTTP endpoint and puts them on an in-memory unbounded queue; 4 workers write to a database. Normal: 2,000 events/s in and out. After a partner migration inflow is 10,000 events/s while the DB handles 2,000/s. Heap is 4 GB; each event is 1 KB. Symptoms: heap grows 8 MB/s, GC time rises from 2% to 70%, p99 ingest latency is 40 s, then pods are OOM-killed and the queue contents are lost; the partner retries everything on connection errors.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure and redesign for the 10,000 events/s case.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase memory" or "add workers." Misses that the downstream is the bottleneck and the queue is unbounded.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can events be lost or sampled? Is order required? Does the partner support 429 and retry with backoff? Can the DB scale or batch writes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Return 429/503 from ingest when the queue passes a limit; ask the partner to throttle; scale the DB writers only if the DB has headroom.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Surplus = 8,000 events/s x 1 KB = 8 MB/s; a 4 GB heap fills in about 8 minutes (matches). GC spirals as the old generation fills. Latency of queued items = queue length / service rate: 600,000 items at 2,000/s is 5 minutes; the real wait was longer.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap graph and -Xlog:gc*, queue depth, DB write latency and CPU, and consumer rate.
  5. Root cause: No backpressure: an unbounded buffer between a fast producer and a slow consumer, plus a lossy failure mode (in-memory data loss on OOM).
  6. Fix: Bound the queue (for example 10,000 items = 10 MB) and reject with 429 plus Retry-After; for durability use Kafka or SQS as the buffer (disk is the bound, lag is the signal); batch DB writes (bulk insert 500 rows) to raise throughput several-fold; scale consumers by partitions only after checking DB capacity.
val ch = Channel<Event>(capacity = 10_000)           // bounded
// producer: ch.trySend(e).isSuccess or respond 429
launch { for (e in ch) batcher.add(e) }               // slow consumer paces the producer
BlockingQueue<Event> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10_000);
if (!q.offer(e)) { return Response.status(429).header("Retry-After", "2").build(); }
  1. Prevention: Alerts on queue depth and age of oldest item; load test with a slow DB; a lint rule against unbounded queues.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Choose block, drop or spill deliberately; Kafka keeps data but lag grows 8 MB/s (28.8 GB/hour), so size retention and add consumers. Not "larger heap".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Telemetry is loss tolerant? -> Sample or drop-oldest instead of rejecting.
  • Autoscaling consumers made the DB fall over? -> Cap concurrency at DB capacity; backpressure must reach the producer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" in-memory buffer became a 3-hour outage; swapping to a bounded queue plus 429 made the next overload a non-event.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more memory or workers.
  • Hire: bounded queue and 429 backpressure.
  • Strong hire: quantifies growth rate, picks durable buffering, batches writes and guards the DB.

questions.contextHtml:
Review this code for a service called by a mobile app with a 2 s user-facing budget. Traffic is 800 req/s; the pricing dependency has p99 of 300 ms normally and 5 s when degraded.

public Price getPrice(String sku) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        try {
            return pricingClient.get(sku);       // client readTimeout = 10s, no breaker
        } catch (Exception e) {
            // retry immediately
        }
    }
    throw new PricingUnavailable();
}
fun getPrice(sku: String): Price {
    repeat(5) {
        try { return pricingClient.get(sku) }   // readTimeout = 10s
        catch (e: Exception) { /* retry immediately */ }
    }
    throw PricingUnavailable()
}
questions.promptHtml: List the defects, estimate the worst-case behaviour and rewrite the call.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a circuit breaker." Does not compute the 50 s worst case or note non-transient errors and idempotency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is get idempotent (yes for reads)? Which exceptions are transient? Is there another retry in the HTTP client or mesh? What fallback is acceptable (cached price)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower the client read timeout to about 400 ms and max attempts to 2, via config.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) worst case 5 x 10 s = 50 s against a 2 s user budget; (b) 5 immediate retries multiply load up to 5x on a sick service (4,000 req/s from 800); (c) catching Exception retries bugs and 4xx; (d) no jitter, no budget; (e) possible hidden retries in the HTTP client or mesh multiply again; (f) no fallback.
  4. How I'd verify each: Look at client config and mesh policy; measure retries per request metric; inject a 5 s dependency delay in staging.
  5. Root cause: Retry and timeout policy chosen independently of the caller's deadline and of the callee's capacity.
  6. Fix: Deadline-aware call: breaker, 1 retry only on transient errors, jittered, per-try timeout 400 ms, whole call within 1.2 s, fallback to cached price flagged as stale.
Supplier<Price> call = Decorators.ofSupplier(() -> pricingClient.get(sku))
    .withCircuitBreaker(breaker)
    .withRetry(retryTwoAttemptsJitter)   // transient exceptions only
    .withFallback(List.of(PricingTimeout.class, CallNotPermittedException.class),
                  e -> priceCache.getStale(sku))
    .decorate();
val call = Decorators.ofSupplier { pricingClient.get(sku) }
    .withCircuitBreaker(breaker)
    .withRetry(retryTwoAttemptsJitter)
    .withFallback(listOf(PricingTimeout::class.java, CallNotPermittedException::class.java)) {
        priceCache.getStale(sku)
    }
    .decorate()

Check the library's decorator order (verify) so the breaker records each attempt as intended. 7. Prevention: Shared client library with defaults; code review rule: every remote call states timeout, retry policy and fallback; fault-injection test. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A stale price may be wrong for pricing; the product team must approve staleness bounds. Do not retry with no limit "to be safe".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• POST instead of GET? -> Add an idempotency key or do not retry.
  • Mesh also retries 2 times? -> Total attempts = 3 x 2; keep one layer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A loop like this turned a 5 s dependency brownout into 4,000 req/s and a full outage of a normally 800 req/s call path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "add a breaker".
  • Hire: quantifies the 50 s and fixes retries and timeouts.
  • Strong hire: ties to the caller's deadline, adds a budgeted breaker and fallback, and a failure test.

questions.contextHtml: The CTO says: "The product page must never be down." The page needs price, inventory, reviews, personalised recommendations and a promo banner, from five services each at 99.9% availability. Today the page is a single orchestrated call; any failure returns an error page. Availability measured: 99.5%. Fraud/auth is not involved in this page.
questions.promptHtml: Ask the right clarifying questions, then design what "never down" means, with numbers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries and a cache everywhere." Does not classify dependencies or test fallbacks.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the actual SLO (99.95%?) and the cost of an outage minute? Which parts are critical for revenue? How stale may price and inventory be (wrong price is a legal issue)? What happens at add-to-cart if inventory is unknown?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn the single call into independent calls with timeouts so one failure does not fail the whole page.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Series availability: 0.999^5 = 99.5% (matches). Classify: price is critical; inventory is important (can show "check at checkout"); reviews, recs and banner are optional. Page availability becomes that of price plus a small contribution from inventory, roughly 99.9%, and with a cached price 99.95% or better.
  4. How I'd verify each: Dependency graph review; fault-injection per dependency in staging; confirm each fallback returns a valid page.
  5. Root cause: All dependencies treated as critical in one orchestration.
  6. Fix: Fallback ladder: stale-while-revalidate cache for price (with a max-age and a flag), default "bestsellers" for recs, hide reviews and banner, show "stock confirmed at checkout" for inventory; separate endpoints or a BFF that fans out in parallel with per-call timeouts; never fail open on security.
  7. Prevention: Chaos experiments (kill each dependency in turn, then in pairs); synthetic page checks; a metric for "degraded responses served" so degradation is visible, not silent.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Stale prices are a business risk; require the checkout path to re-validate price. Do not claim "never down", agree a number like 99.95% and what degraded means.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The cache is also down? -> Last-resort static price snapshot; or fail clearly with a retry.
  • A fallback calls the same failing service? -> That is not a fallback; use independent data.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's fallback path had been broken for months because nothing exercised it; the first real outage exposed a null pointer in the fallback itself.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries and caches everywhere.
  • Hire: classifies critical vs optional with a fallback ladder.
  • Strong hire: asks about the SLO and staleness, does the availability math and plans chaos tests.

questions.contextHtml: A search service calls a ranking service through a Resilience4j breaker: slidingWindowSize: 10, minimumNumberOfCalls: 5, failureRateThreshold: 50, waitDurationInOpenState: 2s, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 1. Traffic is 300 req/s. Logs over 3 minutes: state changes CLOSED -> OPEN -> HALF_OPEN -> OPEN about 40 times; ranking CPU stays at 95%; p99 on search is 1.8 s with intermittent errors. A single bad host in ranking (1 of 12) returns errors 100% of the time. The breaker is one instance for the whole ranking cluster.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the breaker not helping, and how would you reconfigure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The ranking service is down, wait for it." Misses that 11 of 12 hosts are healthy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the failure per host, per endpoint, or global? How are calls load-balanced? What is ranking's real capacity? What fallback exists?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Eject the bad host from the pool and increase the open-state wait to 10 to 30 s to give ranking breathing room.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) window too small (10 calls at 300 req/s is 33 ms of data), so noise trips it; (b) 2 s cool-down hammers a recovering service; (c) a single trial call in half-open is a weak signal; (d) one breaker for the cluster cannot tell a bad host from a bad service; a failing host makes the failure rate hover around 8% (1/12), enough to flap with a tiny window; (e) the 95% CPU suggests ranking is also overloaded.
  4. How I'd verify each: Breaker metrics (state, not-permitted calls); per-host error rate; ranking CPU and queue; replay in staging.
  5. Root cause: Mis-scoped and mis-tuned breaker: it reacts to host-level failure as service failure while giving no relief.
  6. Fix: Use outlier detection at the load balancer/mesh to eject the bad host (Envoy outlier detection); make the breaker window larger (for example time-based 30 s window, minimum 100 calls), waitDurationInOpenState 20 to 30 s, 5 permitted half-open calls, slow-call threshold, and a fallback to cached or default ranking.
slidingWindowType: TIME_BASED
slidingWindowSize: 30
minimumNumberOfCalls: 100
failureRateThreshold: 50
waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5
  1. Prevention: Alert on breaker flapping (more than N transitions per 5 minutes); load test with one bad host; canary the config.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A longer open time delays recovery detection; accept it. Do not disable the breaker. Do not make thresholds so loose it never trips.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should breakers be per host? -> Often use per-host ejection (mesh) plus a per-service breaker.
  • Fallback quality? -> Cached ranking is stale but valid; define staleness limit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A breaker flapping 40 times in 3 minutes kept a half-recovered service in constant restart pressure for an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: waits for the service.
  • Hire: spots window size and cool-down issues.
  • Strong hire: separates host from service failure, tunes with numbers and adds fallback and flapping alerts.

questions.contextHtml: Timeline from a post-incident document: 20:00 a 2-minute traffic spike (3x normal) saturated the order service; 20:02 spike ended but p99 stayed at 12 s and error rate at 35% for 70 minutes. During that time the database cache hit rate dropped from 97% to 40%, clients retried 3 times with no jitter, and the load balancer had ejected 6 of 20 healthy-but-slow pods, concentrating load on the rest. Recovery came at 21:12 when the team blocked traffic at the CDN for 4 minutes, restarted pods, and let traffic ramp. Autoscaler had added 10 pods at 20:08 with no effect.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review: why did the incident outlast its trigger, and what are the action items?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Traffic spike; we need more capacity." Treats the trigger as the cause and ignores the feedback loops.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What was steady-state utilisation? Which loops amplified load (retries, cache misses, ejections)? What data shows each? What did the 4-minute block change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: The effective one was cutting load below capacity, letting caches warm, then ramping gradually.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) retry storm sustained load above capacity; (b) cold cache raised DB work per request, lowering capacity (a capacity drop caused by the incident); (c) outlier ejection of slow pods reduced capacity further (positive feedback); (d) autoscaled pods were cold, joining a saturated system and making it worse.
  4. How I'd verify each: Request amplification ratio over time; cache hit rate vs latency; ejection events; capacity per pod before and after; replay in a load-test.
  5. Root cause: A metastable failure: the system had a stable bad state sustained by feedback loops, even after the trigger ended. The trigger is not the root cause; the loops are.
  6. Fix: Retry budget with jitter; load shedding and per-request deadline drops; cap outlier ejection percentage (for example at most 20% of hosts); warm-up and slow-start for new pods; cache protection (single flight, stale-while-revalidate); an operator "pressure valve" runbook: reduce traffic first, then restore, then ramp.
  7. Prevention: Game day replaying a 3x spike; alert on goodput not just errors; load test beyond capacity and verify recovery without human action; headroom policy (for example 30% at peak).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More capacity helps only if the loops are broken; blanket over-provisioning is expensive. No blame on the on-call who used the CDN block; it worked.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could autoscaling have helped? -> Only with slow-start and warm caches; scale-out into a retry storm can hit the DB harder.
  • Is this really different from a normal overload? -> Normal overload ends when load falls; metastable failure persists after the trigger.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The incident report listed "traffic spike" as root cause until someone plotted offered load: it was back to normal 68 minutes before the recovery.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the spike, asks for more capacity.
  • Hire: identifies retries and cold cache as sustaining loops.
  • Strong hire: names metastability, maps the loops, adds budgets, ejection caps and a tested recovery runbook.
